medical-reference-document.title: MedlinePlus Health Topic: Diabetes
medical-reference-document.publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM / NIH)

sections.section: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by elevated levels of blood glucose (hyperglycemia), which leads over time to serious damage to the heart, blood vessels, eyes, kidneys and nerves. Glucose is derived from food intake and insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas that allows cells to absorb glucose for energy. In Type 1 diabetes, autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells results in an absolute deficiency of insulin. In Type 2 diabetes, the body develops insulin resistance combined with progressive impairment of insulin secretion. Prediabetes is an intermediate state of hyperglycemia with glycemic parameters above normal but below clinical diagnostic thresholds for diabetes.

section.title: Diabetes Mellitus - Symptoms and Diagnostic Criteria

sections.section: Common clinical symptoms of diabetes include polyuria (excessive urination), polydipsia (excessive thirst), polyphagia (constant hunger), unexplained weight loss, generalized fatigue, blurred vision, and slow-healing cutaneous sores. Diagnostic criteria per clinical guidelines require one of the following laboratory confirmations: 1. Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) greater than or equal to 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after an 8-hour fast. 2. Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) greater than or equal to 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) using a certified standardized assay. 3. 2-hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) 75g post-load glucose greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L). 4. Random plasma glucose greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL in a patient exhibiting classic symptoms of hyperglycemia.

Effective management of diabetes requires routine self-monitoring of blood glucose, comprehensive lifestyle interventions including medical nutrition therapy, structured physical activity (at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise), and weight management. Pharmacological management for Type 2 diabetes initiates with oral Metformin in the absence of contraindications, with sequential escalation to SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, or exogenous basal-bolus insulin. Chronic microvascular complications comprise diabetic retinopathy, diabetic nephropathy, and diabetic peripheral/autonomic neuropathy. Macrovascular complications include coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, and cerebrovascular stroke.
